job.system:
You are the AI assistant for Meridian Ocean Minerals. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Meridian Ocean Minerals is a deep-sea mining company headquartered in Houston, with a policy office in Washington, DC. Our mission is to commercially recover polymetallic nodules from the deep seabed, a vast source of nickel, cobalt, manganese, and copper, and to supply these critical minerals for batteries, the energy transition, and economic growth. We believe the United States must lead in this industry. Our policy team works with lawmakers to protect our ability to continue exploration and commercial development.

Current focus: Our top priority this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act, which would shut down our core work and which we strongly oppose. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup, can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
Here are the issues I found, grouped by type. They are numbered continuously for easy reference at markup. I reviewed only the text you provided, not the pre-amendment version or the cited statutes, so have counsel verify the cross-references (items 6, 7, 28, 29).

## A. Gaps that could let activity continue

1. **§2(1)(A), threshold and "single vessel."** The 10,000 t/yr test applies per vessel, so an operator can run several vessels each under the threshold, or rotate vessels, and never trigger the prohibition. The threshold is also tiny compared with commercial-scale plans.
2. **§2(1)(A), undefined measurement terms.** "Recovery," "per year" (calendar or rolling 12 months), and the weight basis (wet or dry; nodules hold significant moisture) are all undefined. Stockpiling on the seabed, or lifting by a tender or collector vehicle rather than the "vessel," may fall outside "recovery by a single vessel."
3. **§2(2), narrow "U.S. person."** It covers only citizens and State-organized corporations, so it omits LLCs, partnerships, trusts, and other non-corporate entities, as well as lawful permanent residents and DC- or territory-organized entities. It has no ownership or control test, so foreign-incorporated subsidiaries of U.S. companies fall outside it.
4. **§3(a), reach of the prohibition.** It applies only to persons "in the United States" or U.S. persons, so foreign-flag vessels and foreign affiliates working outside U.S. territory escape it. "Engage in" is undefined and may not reach financing, offtake, processing, or importing nodules mined elsewhere.
5. **§3(a)/§2(1), "commercial" is purely volume-based.** Nothing about sale, profit, or intent matters, so an operation staying below the volume line, or structured as pilot or research work, is outside the prohibition regardless of its purpose.
6. **§3(b), grandfathering scope.** It exempts "mining conducted under an exploration license," but exploration licenses are generally not authorizations for commercial recovery. That leaves it unclear what is exempt, and whether holders of commercial recovery permits (if any) are covered at all.
7. **§3(b), undefined "exploration license."** It does not say who issued the license (NOAA, a foreign state, or an ISA sponsor) or whether renewals, amendments, area expansions, transfers, or extensions stay exempt. As drafted, the exemption has no end date or compliance condition and could be indefinite.
8. **§3(b), heading and text mismatch.** The heading says "Existing Operations," but the text keys only on the license issue date, not on whether operations had actually begun. That invites disputes over what is "existing."
9. **§3(c), environmental assessment exemption.** "Environmental assessment" is undefined, with no cap on volume, duration, or area, no ban on selling or processing recovered material, and no notice or permit requirement. A "for the purpose of" test is subjective and easy to claim for test mining or bulk sampling.
10. **§8 and §3, 180-day delay.** The prohibition does not take effect for 180 days after enactment, leaving a window to ramp up operations, accumulate stockpiles, or restructure. The bill does not say whether activity begun in the window is covered after the effective date.
11. **§2(3)/§4, vessel size cutoff.** Only vessels over 5,000 gross tons must register, so smaller vessels face no registry or reporting. "Equipped for the recovery" is ambiguous: it is unclear whether chartered, converted, or support vessels count.
12. **§7(b), sunset.** A 10-year sunset (about 9.5 effective years given §8) invites a wait-out strategy. It also has no savings clause, so pending enforcement of pre-sunset violations could be argued to lapse.

## B. Enforcement and administrability problems

13. **§2(1)(B), §4, undefined "Secretary."** The bill never says which Secretary. It is unclear who makes the §2(1)(B) determinations or who runs enforcement.
14. **§3 and §5, no designated enforcement authority.** No agency is assigned to investigate or enforce §3, and there is no rulemaking authority, administrative adjudication process, DOJ referral mechanism, or Coast Guard role.
15. **§5(a), no civil enforcement tools.** There is no grant of district court jurisdiction, no injunctive relief, and no authority to seize or forfeit vessels, equipment, or recovered minerals. Penalties alone may not stop an operation.
16. **§4, no consequences for registry violations.** §5 penalizes only violations of §3, so failure to register, late reports, or false certifications carry no stated penalty. There are also no registration deadlines, forms, or fees.
17. **§4(b), weak reporting content.** Reports need only "describe recovery activities." They need not state tonnage, location, depth, dates, or destination of material, so they cannot show whether the §2(1)(A) threshold was crossed. There is also no audit, inspection, or verification authority, and "certified by the operator" has no standard.
18. **§3 and §4, mismatch.** The prohibition turns on tonnage and §2(1)(B) determinations, while the registry turns on vessel size. Grandfathered operators are not distinguished from prohibited ones, so the registry cannot identify violations.
19. **§5(a) and §8, conflicting dates.** Civil penalties apply to violations "on or after the date of enactment," but the Act takes effect 180 days later. This creates ambiguity over whether penalties can accrue in the gap, and it invites fair-notice defenses.
20. **§5(a), "each day."** The bill does not say whether a continuous operation is one violation or one per day, or how multiple vessels are counted. There is also no inflation adjustment.
21. **§5(b), "willfully."** It is undefined, so defendants can argue it requires knowledge that the conduct was unlawful. That is especially hard to prove when applicability depends on §2(1)(B) determinations. The section also has no organizational liability provision and no criminal false-statement offense tied to §4.
22. **§3(a), proof across borders.** Establishing tonnage, depth, and the vessel's identity for activity far offshore will be hard without the §4 data, and there is no evidence-gathering or international cooperation mechanism.
23. **§6, precatory.** The Secretary of State need only "seek to negotiate," with no definition of "equivalent" prohibitions, no reporting to Congress, and no consequence for missing the 18-month deadline. It is also unclear whether the deadline modifies "seek" or "negotiate."
24. **§7(a), no mechanism for the NAS report.** The National Academies are not directed, funded, or given a deadline to produce the report. "Serious harm" is undefined, and it is unclear whether a joint resolution lifts the prohibition automatically or requires further action.
25. **§7(a) and §7(b), internal inconsistency.** Subsection (a) makes the prohibition last until Congress acts, while (b) ends the Act after 10 years regardless. This makes (a) largely meaningless and creates confusion over which controls.
26. **General, no severability clause.** If a court strikes any provision (for example, §2(1)(B) or the extraterritorial reach), nothing says the rest survives.

## C. Vulnerabilities to legal challenge

27. **§2(1)(B), vagueness and delegation.** "Risks … comparable to" the §2(1)(A) activities is a standardless, undefined test, applied by an unnamed Secretary with no rulemaking, notice, or published criteria. Because §5(b) attaches criminal liability, this is vulnerable on fair-notice and nondelegation grounds.
28. **§2(1)(A), overbreadth and statutory overlap.** The 200 m depth line matches the continental shelf edge, not the deep seabed, and "other mineral resources" is undefined. Together they could sweep in sand and gravel dredging or other offshore activity, and they overlap with OCSLA leasing and DSHMRA licensing. The bill does not amend or reconcile those statutes, which raises implied-repeal and conflict questions.
29. **§3(b), takings and due process.** Applicants with pending license applications, and any holders of commercial recovery permits not clearly covered by the exemption, have investment-backed expectation arguments. The line at "issued before enactment" is also arbitrary and could draw equal-treatment claims.
30. **§5(a), excessive fines.** Up to $1,000,000 per day, with no proportionality factors or ability-to-pay considerations, is open to an Eighth Amendment challenge.
31. **§3(a), international law and extraterritoriality.** Applying U.S. law to U.S. persons aboard foreign-flag vessels, or in areas beyond national jurisdiction, invites flag-state and high-seas-freedom objections. The bill has no findings or statement of congressional intent on extraterritorial application.
32. **§7(a), joint resolution.** A joint resolution must be presented to the President, so a veto could block lifting the prohibition. A sitting Congress also cannot bind a later one to the NAS-report process, so the clause is of doubtful legal effect.
33. **General, no findings or record.** The bill contains no findings on the environmental harm it targets, which weakens its defense against arbitrary-and-capricious or rational-basis challenges and gives courts little guidance on interpretation.

## Most useful for markup

The highest-impact items for the policy team are likely these:
- Vagueness and delegation in §2(1)(B) (item 27).
- Conflicting dates between §5(a) and §8 (item 19).
- The undefined and open-ended §3(b) and §3(c) exemptions (items 6–9).
- The absence of any enforcement authority or procedures (items 13–16).
- The §7(a)/§7(b) inconsistency (item 25).

Some of these are exactly the issues sponsors may try to fix with a further manager's amendment, so consider which you want to raise publicly and which to hold.
